claim: All vertebrate brains possess three major divisions: the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon), and hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
source: It is accepted that all vertebrate brains possess three major divisions: the forebrain (prosencephalon), midbrain (mesencephalon), and hindbrain (rhombencephalon).
evidence: This is stated as an accepted fact in the scientific community, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Brain morphogenesis established along the anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral axes of the neural tube occurs at early embryonic states.
source: The brain morphogenesis established along the anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral axes of the neural tube occurs at early embryonic states (Figdor and Stern, 1993; Joyner et al., 2000; Echevarría et al., 2003; Stern et al., 2006; Vieira et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Neuronal connectivity that determines brain functions is established at later developmental stages.
source: Neuronal connectivity that determines the brain functions is established at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle based on established knowledge.

claim: There is no consensus on the regional homology of related brain structures across vertebrate species.
source: Yet, there is no consensus on the regional homology of the related brain structures across species.
evidence: This reflects the current state of scientific debate in the field.

claim: Several different thalamic nuclei in birds convey sensory information to the pallium in a modality-specific manner.
source: Notably in birds, several different thalamic nuclei convey sensory information to the pallium (Pal; dorsal telencephalon containing the cortex in mammals) in a modality-specific manner.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about avian neuroanatomy.

claim: The avian thalamo-pallial pathway is often compared to the mammalian thalamocortical pathway.
source: Thus, the avian thalamo-pallial pathway is often compared to the mammalian thalamocortical pathway (Figure 1; amniotes; Th → Pal) (Butler, 1994a; Butler, 1994b; Reiner et al., 2005).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Homology of the target pallial areas in birds has been under debate.
source: In contrast, homology of the target pallial areas has been under debate (Karten and Shimizu, 1989; Bruce and Neary, 1995; Striedter, 1997; Puelles et al., 2000; Butler et al., 2011; Dugas-Ford et al., 2012).
evidence: Multiple citations indicate ongoing scientific debate.

claim: In amphibians, sensory projections from the thalamus mainly terminate in the subpallium with little projections to the pallium.
source: Amphibians are the closest outgroup, but unlike amniotes, their sensory projections from the thalamus (Th) mainly terminate in the subpallium (SPa; ventral telencephalon containing the striatum; Figure 1; amphibians; Th → SPa), with little projections to the pallium (Kicliter, 1979; Neary and Northcutt, 1983; Wilczynski and Northcutt, 1983; Butler, 1994a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Teleosts have sensory afferents to the pallium.
source: Although teleosts also have sensory afferents to the pallium, the morphology of the teleost pallium is very different from that of tetrapods, as the developmental processes are different (evagination in tetrapods versus eversion in teleosts).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about teleost neuroanatomy.

claim: The developmental processes of the pallium differ between tetrapods (evagination) and teleosts (eversion).
source: Although teleosts also have sensory afferents to the pallium, the morphology of the teleost pallium is very different from that of tetrapods, as the developmental processes are different (evagination in tetrapods versus eversion in teleosts).
evidence: This is stated as an established difference in developmental biology.

claim: Different authors have proposed different hypotheses concerning which part of the teleost pallium corresponds to the mammalian neocortex.
source: Different authors have proposed different hypotheses concerning which part of the teleost pallium would correspond to the mammalian neocortex (Braford, 1995; Wullimann and Mueller, 2004; Northcutt, 2006; Yamamoto et al., 2007; Yamamoto, 2009; Mueller et al., 2011).
evidence: Multiple citations indicate ongoing scientific debate.

claim: Recent publications examining developmental processes of the zebrafish pallium have modified the classical view of the eversion model.
source: Recent publications examining developmental processes of the zebrafish pallium have modified the classical view of the eversion model (Folgueira et al., 2012; Dirian et al., 2014; Furlan et al., 2017), and we have proposed a new interpretation on the pallial homology (Yamamoto and Bloch, 2017; Yamamoto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: It has been debated whether or not the structure giving rise to the major pallial projections in teleosts is homologous to the tetrapod thalamus.
source: It has also been debated whether or not the structure giving rise to the major pallial projections is homologous to the tetrapod thalamus (Wullimann and Rink, 2002; Northcutt, 2006; Yamamoto and Ito, 2008; Mueller, 2012).
evidence: Multiple citations indicate ongoing scientific debate.

claim: The structure giving rise to major pallial projections in teleosts is named the preglomerular complex (PG).
source: This structure is named the preglomerular complex (PG; Figure 1; teleosts; PG → Pal).
evidence: This is stated as a nomenclature fact and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The teleost PG has been considered to originate from the basal portion of the diencephalon, the posterior tuberculum, based on descriptive embryology.
source: On the one hand, based on descriptive embryology, the teleost PG has been considered to originate from the basal portion of the diencephalon, the posterior tuberculum (Bergquist, 1932; Braford and Northcutt, 1983; Butler and Hodos, 2005; Northcutt, 2008; Vernier and Wullimann, 2009).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The thalamus originates from the alar portion of the diencephalon.
source: In contrast, the thalamus originates from the alar portion of the diencephalon.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about thalamic development.

claim: It has been proposed that PG may be homologous to the thalamus due to similar connectivity patterns of sensory pathways.
source: On the other hand, due to the similar connectivity patterns of sensory pathways, it has also been proposed that PG may be homologous to the thalamus (Yamamoto and Ito, 2008; Ito and Yamamoto, 2009).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The PG receives various sensory inputs of different modalities including visual, auditory, lateral line, gustatory, and possibly somatosensory.
source: The PG receives various sensory inputs of different modalities (e.g. visual, auditory, lateral line, gustatory, and possibly somatosensory), and gives rise to ascending projections to the pallium (Striedter, 1991; Striedter, 1992; Yoshimoto et al., 1998; Yamamoto and Ito, 2005; Yamamoto and Ito, 2008; Northcutt, 2006; Ito and Yamamoto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The PG gives rise to ascending projections to the pallium.
source: The PG receives various sensory inputs of different modalities (e.g. visual, auditory, lateral line, gustatory, and possibly somatosensory), and gives rise to ascending projections to the pallium (Striedter, 1991; Striedter, 1992; Yoshimoto et al., 1998; Yamamoto and Ito, 2005; Yamamoto and Ito, 2008; Northcutt, 2006; Ito and Yamamoto, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In goldfish and carp, the lateral preglomerular nucleus (PGl) receives visual information from the optic tectum and projects to the lateral part of the dorsal telencephalic area (Dl) within the pallium.
source: In goldfish and carp, the lateral preglomerular nucleus (PGl), a component nucleus within the PG, receives visual information from the optic tectum (TeO) and projects to the lateral part of the dorsal telencephalic area (Dl) within the pallium (TeO → PG → Pal; Figure 1; Yamamoto and Ito, 2005; Yamamoto and Ito, 2008; Northcutt, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The tectofugal visual pathway in goldfish and carp is similar to the tectofugal or extrageniculate visual pathway in mammals.
source: This is similar to the tectofugal or extrageniculate visual pathway in mammals: a visual thalamic nucleus (pulvinar in primates, and lateral posterior nucleus in other mammals like rodents) receives inputs from the TeO (superior colliculus -SC- in mammals) and projects to the visual pallium (extrastriate visual cortex in mammals) (SC → Th → Pal; Figure 1).
evidence: This comparison is based on established knowledge of mammalian neuroanatomy and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The relative size and complexity of the PG are correlated with the complexity of the pallial connections.
source: In addition, the relative size and complexity of the PG are correlated with the complexity of the pallial connections, similarly to what has been documented in the tetrapod thalamus (Northcutt, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some studies have suggested that the PG consists of Pax6-positive alar diencephalic cells that migrate ventrally during development.
source: Some other studies have suggested that the PG consists of Pax6-positive (Pax6+) alar diencephalic cells that migrate ventrally during development (Wullimann and Puelles, 1999; Wullimann and Rink, 2001; Wullimann and Rink, 2002; Mueller and Wullimann, 2002; Ishikawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: A cell lineage study in zebrafish has shown that many PG cells are migrating from the midbrain region, instead of the diencephalon.
source: More recently, our cell lineage study in zebrafish has shown that many PG cells are migrating from the midbrain region, instead of the diencephalon (which is in the forebrain).
evidence: This is based on the authors' own previous research.

claim: The ventral brain regions containing the PG, the torus lateralis (TLa), and the inferior lobe (IL) are composed of cells migrating from the midbrain-hindbrain boundary (MHB).
source: The ventral brain regions containing the PG, the torus lateralis (TLa), and the inferior lobe (IL), which were considered to be part of the forebrain, are in fact composed of cells migrating from the midbrain-hindbrain boundary (MHB) (Bloch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous research.

claim: The data strongly suggest that the PG is not, as a whole, homologous to the amniote thalamus.
source: These data strongly suggest that the PG is not, as a whole, homologous to the amniote thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cell lineage data.

claim: The Tg(gSAGFF279A) transgenic line crossed with Tg(UAS:GFP) has GFP-positive cells projecting to a part of the pallium.
source: Among these lines, we identified a Gal4-expressing transgenic fish line, Tg(gSAGFF279A) crossed with Tg(UAS: GFP), which had GFP-positive (GFP+) cells projecting to a part of the pallium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gene trap construct in Tg(gSAGFF279A) was integrated within an intron of the inpp5ka gene.
source: We analyzed the genomic DNA from the transgenic fish by Southern blot and inverse PCR, and found that the gene trap construct was integrated within an intron of the inpp5ka (inositol polyphosphate-5-phosphatase Ka) gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on molecular analysis and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the Tg(279A-GFP) line, abundant GFP+ fibers are present in the Dl.
source: In the Tg(279A-GFP), abundant GFP+ fibers are present in the Dl (Figure 2A), and GFP+ cell bodies are found in a part of PG (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the Tg(279A-GFP) line, GFP+ cell bodies are found in a part of PG.
source: In the Tg(279A-GFP), abundant GFP+ fibers are present in the Dl (Figure 2A), and GFP+ cell bodies are found in a part of PG (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Axonal projections originating from the PG terminate in the ipsilateral Dl.
source: We confirmed that axonal projections originating from the PG terminate in the ipsilateral Dl (Figure 2C and Video 1).
evidence: This is based on 3D reconstruction of confocal images shown in Figure 2C and Video 1.

claim: The projection from the PG to the Dl in zebrafish is similar to the ascending visual projection of other cyprinid species such as goldfish and carp.
source: This projection from the PG to the Dl is quite similar to the ascending visual projection of other cyprinid species such as goldfish and carp (Yamamoto and Ito, 2008).
evidence: This comparison is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In goldfish and carp, the vast majority of retinal axons terminate in TeO, and the TeO neurons project to the PGl, which in turn projects to the Dl in the pallium.
source: In goldfish and carp, the vast majority of retinal axons terminate in TeO, and the TeO neurons project to the PGl, which in turn projects to the Dl in the pallium.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about goldfish and carp neuroanatomy.

claim: The PGl-Dl projection is not yet observable at 4 weeks post-fertilization (wpf).
source: The PGl-Dl projection is not yet observable at 4 weeks post-fertilization (wpf) (Figure 3A,B, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A few GFP+ cell bodies appear at the level of PG around 6 wpf.
source: A few GFP+ cell bodies appear at the level of PG around 6 wpf.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: The GFP+ cell cluster in PG becomes prominent at 8 wpf.
source: The GFP+ cell cluster in PG (which we consider as PGl) becomes prominent at 8 wpf (Figure 3D), yet the GFP+ fiber labeling in the Dl appear very weak at this stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At 8 wpf, the GFP+ fiber labeling in the Dl appears very weak.
source: The GFP+ cell cluster in PG (which we consider as PGl) becomes prominent at 8 wpf (Figure 3D), yet the GFP+ fiber labeling in the Dl appear very weak at this stage (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: At 3 months post-fertilization (mpf), there are around 200 GFP+ cells in the PG in each side of the brain.
source: At 3 months post-fertilization (mpf), there are around 200 GFP+ cells in the PG in each side of the brain (Figure 2B–D, Figure 3F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), and they project heavily to the Dl (Figure 2A,C,D, Figure 3E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in multiple figures.

claim: At 3 mpf, PG cells project heavily to the Dl.
source: At 3 months post-fertilization (mpf), there are around 200 GFP+ cells in the PG in each side of the brain (Figure 2B–D, Figure 3F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1I), and they project heavily to the Dl (Figure 2A,C,D, Figure 3E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,F).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in multiple figures.

claim: Retinal projections terminate in the upper layers of TeO in zebrafish.
source: It has been known that retinal projections terminate in the upper layers of TeO in a wide range of species of ray-finned fish (von Bartheld and Meyer, 1987), and it is also the case in zebrafish (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: DiI injection into the PGl resulted in retrogradely labeled cell bodies in a deep layer of TeO.
source: After 2–3 weeks of incubation, we observed retrogradely labeled cell bodies in a deep layer of TeO (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on tract-tracing experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Retrogradely labeled neurons in TeO extend dendrites up to the retino-recipient upper layer of TeO (SFGS).
source: Each cell extends its dendrites up to the retino-recipient upper layer of TeO (the stratum fibrosum et griseum superficiale; SFGS), and this morphology is identical to the neurons receiving retinal inputs in carp and goldfish (Yamamoto and Ito, 2008).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and comparison with previous research.

claim: BDA injections into the TeO labeled axon terminals in the PGl.
source: BDA injections into the TeO (Figure 4C, asterisk) labeled axon terminals in the PGl (Figure 4D, arrowheads), confirming that the PGl receives tectal inputs.
evidence: This is based on tract-tracing experiments shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: The PGl receives tectal inputs.
source: BDA injections into the TeO (Figure 4C, asterisk) labeled axon terminals in the PGl (Figure 4D, arrowheads), confirming that the PGl receives tectal inputs.
evidence: This is confirmed by tract-tracing experiments shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Biocytin injection into PGl resulted in abundant fiber labeling in the Dl.
source: Following the biocytin injection into PGl (Figure 4G, asterisk), we observed abundant fiber labeling in the Dl (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is based on tract-tracing experiments shown in Figure 4G and 4H.

claim: The Dl labeling pattern from biocytin injection is identical to the GFP+ fiber labeling of the Tg(279A-GFP).
source: This Dl labeling pattern is identical to the GFP+ fiber labeling of the Tg(279A-GFP) (Figure 2A and Figure 4I).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4I.

claim: Biocytin injections into Dl labeled perikarya of PGl neurons.
source: Conversely, biocytin injections into Dl (Figure 4J, asterisk) labeled perikarya of PGl neurons (Figure 4K), coinciding with the position of the GFP+ cells in Tg(279A-GFP) (Figure 4L, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on tract-tracing experiments shown in Figure 4J and 4K.

claim: The position of biocytin-labeled PGl neurons coincides with the position of GFP+ cells in Tg(279A-GFP).
source: Conversely, biocytin injections into Dl (Figure 4J, asterisk) labeled perikarya of PGl neurons (Figure 4K), coinciding with the position of the GFP+ cells in Tg(279A-GFP) (Figure 4L, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 4K and 4L.

claim: The PGl conveys visual information from the TeO to the Dl.
source: Thus, we conclude that the PGl conveys visual information from the TeO to the Dl, and that the GFP+ projection from the PG to the Dl in Tg(279A-GFP) recapitulates this visual pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tract-tracing experiments described.

claim: The GFP+ projection from the PG to the Dl in Tg(279A-GFP) recapitulates the visual pathway from TeO to Dl.
source: Thus, we conclude that the PGl conveys visual information from the TeO to the Dl, and that the GFP+ projection from the PG to the Dl in Tg(279A-GFP) recapitulates this visual pathway.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the tract-tracing experiments and transgenic line characterization.

claim: Many cells of mesencephalic origin are present in brain structures that have been considered to be of prosencephalic origin.
source: Based on a cell lineage method using tamoxifen inducible Cre-lox recombination, we recently demonstrated that many cells of mesencephalic (midbrain) origin are present in some brain structures that have been considered to be of prosencephalic (forebrain) origin (Bloch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous research cited.

claim: PG was one of the brain structures containing cells of mesencephalic origin.
source: PG was one of them, thus we further investigated the development of PG cells, including those in PGl.
evidence: This is stated based on the authors' previous research.

claim: The transcription factor her5 is exclusively expressed in the midbrain-hindbrain boundary (MHB) at 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf).
source: The transcription factor her5 is exclusively expressed in the midbrain-hindbrain boundary (MHB) at 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf) (Figure 5A), and in ventricular cell clusters in the midbrain (alar part such as the tectum) at juvenile stages (Galant et al., 2016; Bloch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 5A and supported by citations.

claim: her5 is expressed in ventricular cell clusters in the midbrain (alar part such as the tectum) at juvenile stages.
source: The transcription factor her5 is exclusively expressed in the midbrain-hindbrain boundary (MHB) at 24 hr post-fertilization (hpf) (Figure 5A), and in ventricular cell clusters in the midbrain (alar part such as the tectum) at juvenile stages (Galant et al., 2016; Bloch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PG is constituted as the most rostro-ventral end of a cell cluster migrating from the MHB.
source: By following the mCherry-positive (mCherry+) cells at different developmental stages after induction at 24 hpf, we observe that PG is constituted as the most rostro-ventral end of a cell cluster migrating from the MHB (Figure 5B,D,F and Video 2).
evidence: This is based on cell lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 5B,D,F and Video 2.

claim: The her5-mCherry+ cells are distributed in the entire PG, including the PGl where the 279A-GFP+ pallial projection neurons are located.
source: The her5-mCherry+ cells are distributed in the entire PG, including the PGl where the 279A-GFP+ pallial projection neurons are located (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Many of PG cells, if not all, are of midbrain origin.
source: Thus, we conclude that many of PG cells, if not all, are of midbrain origin.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the cell lineage tracing experiments.

claim: There are GFP+ PG cells co-expressing mCherry in the quadruple transgenic line at adult stage (3 mpf).
source: Observing the PG in the adult stage (3 mpf), we found that there are GFP+ PG cells co-expressing mCherry (Figure 6C–F, arrowheads).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 6C–F.

claim: At least some of the GFP+ pallial projection neurons originate from the MHB.
source: This suggests that at least some of the GFP+ pallial projection neurons originate from the MHB.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization of GFP and mCherry in PG cells.

claim: The expression of Cre in Tg(Dr830:ERT2CreERT2) is limited to the tectal area after 30–48 hpf.
source: In this line, the expression territory of Cre is larger than Tg(her5:ERT2CreERT2) at 24 hpf, but the expression is limited to the tectal area after 30–48 hpf (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tamoxifen treatments induced mCherry expression in many cells in the PG including the PGl.
source: Similarly to the cases using Tg(her5:ERT2CreERT2), tamoxifen treatments induced mCherry expression in many cells in the PG including the PGl.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: At least 60% of PG cells would originate from the midbrain region.
source: Counting mCherry+ cells from individuals induced at different time points suggests that at least 60% of PG cells would originate from the midbrain region (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on quantification of mCherry+ cells shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: GFP/mCherry co-expressing cells were found consistently at all induction time-points until 6 wpf.
source: We found GFP/mCherry co-expressing cells consistently at all the induction time-points until 6 wpf (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 8.

claim: At 6 wpf, there were very few mCherry+ cells in PG, and only one cell co-expressing GFP and mCherry was found among all specimens examined.
source: At 6 wpf, there were very few mCherry+ cells in PG, and we found only one cell co-expressing GFP and mCherry among all the specimens examined (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 8G.

claim: No GFP/mCherry co-expression was observed in the case of induction at 8 wpf.
source: We didn't observe any co-expression in the case of induction at 8 wpf.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: GFP+ PGl cells are gradually added throughout the larval/juvenile stages around up to 6 wpf.
source: Thus, our results suggest that GFP+ PGl cells are gradually added throughout the larval/juvenile stages around up to 6 wpf.
evidence: This is inferred from the tamoxifen induction experiments at different time points.

claim: The majority of GFP+ pallial projection neurons are progenies of cells derived from the tectal region.
source: Considering the small number of GFP+ cells in PGl and the short-term tamoxifen induction time, it would be reasonable to conclude that the majority of GFP+ pallial projection neurons are progenies of cells derived from the tectal region.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data and reasoning about the induction protocol.

claim: The abundance of mCherry+ cells in the adult PG suggests that the majority of PG cells derive from the mesencephalic region.
source: The abundance of mCherry+ cells in the adult PG suggests that the majority of PG cells derive from the mesencephalic region.
evidence: This is inferred from the cell lineage tracing experiments.

claim: PG cells were consistently labeled with mCherry following treatments at all developmental stages examined.
source: PG cells were consistently labeled with mCherry following the treatments at all the developmental stages examined.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation across multiple time points.

claim: PG progressively grows by addition of cells migrating from the mesencephalon.
source: This suggests that PG progressively grows by addition of cells migrating from the mesencephalon.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PG cells are labeled at all developmental stages examined.

claim: Long term tamoxifen treatment leads to a high mortality rate of the fish during the experiment.
source: Long term tamoxifen treatment leads to a high mortality rate of the fish during the experiment (Bloch et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The Cre-lox system would not allow 100% induction rate.
source: Moreover, the Cre-lox system would not allow 100% induction rate (Hayashi and McMahon, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mCherry labeling of each experiment would represent only a fraction of the cells originating from the mesencephalic region.
source: Thus, mCherry labeling of each experiment would represent only a fraction of the cells originating from the mesencephalic region.
evidence: This is inferred from the technical limitations of the tamoxifen induction and Cre-lox system.

claim: There are only about 200 GFP+ neurons in the adult PG.
source: With the use of the Tg(279A-GFP), we could label visual pallial projection neurons in the PG (or more specifically in the PGl). There are only about 200 GFP+ neurons in the adult PG.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation and quantification.

claim: At least one or two GFP/mCherry co-expressing cells were observed consistently whenever tamoxifen induction was performed before 6 wpf.
source: In the quadruple transgenic lines expressing both GFP and mCherry, we observed consistently at least one or two co-expressing cells whenever the tamoxifen induction was performed before 6 wpf.
evidence: This is based on experimental observation across multiple induction time points.

claim: Most of the GFP+ cells may originate from the midbrain.
source: Considering the short duration of each tamoxifen treatment, most of the GFP+ cells may originate from the midbrain.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design and observations.

claim: The PGl projection neurons are mainly composed of cells migrating from the mesencephalon, by gradual accumulation from embryonic to juvenile stages (until around 6 wpf).
source: Thus, we conclude that the PGl projection neurons are mainly composed of cells migrating from the mesencephalon, by gradual accumulation from embryonic to juvenile stages (until around 6 wpf).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the cell lineage tracing experiments at multiple time points.

claim: The absence of mCherry/GFP co-localization at 8 wpf suggests that the PGl reaches maturation around this stage.
source: The absence of mCherry/GFP co-localization at 8 wpf suggests that the PGl reaches maturation around this stage, as indicated by the abundance of projections to the Dl (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: At early embryonic stages (before 30 hpf) in both quadruple transgenic lines, the Cre expression appears to extend from dorsal to ventral MHB.
source: At early embryonic stages (before 30 hpf) in both quadruple transgenic lines, the Cre expression appears to extend from dorsal to ventral MHB, therefore it is hard to conclude whether the PG cells derive from the alar or basal portion.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claim: A recent publication using shh-GFP transgenic line suggests that the adult PG contains shh-expressing cells, indicating that some PG cells may be of basal origin.
source: A recent publication using shh-GFP transgenic line suggests that the adult PG contains shh-expressing cells (GFP+ in the transgenic line), indicating that some PG cells may be of basal origin (Wullimann and Umeasalugo, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: The expression of Cre at later stages (after 48 hpf) is limited to the alar portion of the mesencephalon (notably tectal area).
source: In contrast, the expression of Cre at later stages (after 48 hpf) is limited to the alar portion of the mesencephalon (notably tectal area).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claim: PG cells are migrating from the alar mesencephalic region at least after larval stages.
source: Thus, PG cells are migrating from the alar mesencephalic region at least after larval stages.
evidence: This is inferred from the Cre expression pattern at later stages.

claim: Both thalamic and tectal regions are Pax6+ domains.
source: This is consistent with previous studies claiming the PG is comprised of Pax6-expressing migrating cells (Wullimann and Rink, 2001; Ishikawa et al., 2007): both thalamic and tectal regions are Pax6+ domains.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: The main argument for the forebrain origin of the PG is an indication of radial organization from the diencephalic ventricular zone to the putative PG region.
source: The main argument of the forebrain origin of the PG is an indication of radial organization from the diencephalic ventricular zone to the putative PG region (Wullimann and Rink, 2002; Ishikawa et al., 2007; Mueller and Guo, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The trajectory of PG cell migration was not clearly demonstrated in the present study.
source: In our data, trajectory of the migration was not clearly demonstrated, and we cannot exclude that some PG cells are radially migrated from the diencephalic ventricular zone.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the current study.

claim: Some radially migrated cells may serve as a scaffold at an early stage, and mesencephalic cells by tangential migration may accumulate on them.
source: Thus, we cannot rule out the possibility that some radially migrated cells serve as a scaffold at an early stage, and mesencephalic cells by tangential migration may accumulate on them.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility acknowledged by the authors.

claim: GFP+ fiber labeling in Dl appears to be prominent only at around 8 wpf.
source: GFP+ fiber labeling in Dl appears to be prominent only at around 8 wpf (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The thalamocortical projections in amniotes are already abundant at late embryonic stages.
source: Unlike the thalamocortical projections in amniotes that are already abundant at late embryonic stages (Cordery and Molnár, 1999; Bielle et al., 2011; Molnár et al., 2012), the visual ascending projections to the pallium in zebrafish are not mature until late juvenile stages.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on amniotes.

claim: The visual ascending projections to the pallium in zebrafish are not mature until late juvenile stages.
source: Unlike the thalamocortical projections in amniotes that are already abundant at late embryonic stages (Cordery and Molnár, 1999; Bielle et al., 2011; Molnár et al., 2012), the visual ascending projections to the pallium in zebrafish are not mature until late juvenile stages.
evidence: This is based on the experimental observations in the current study.

claim: Zebrafish larvae can coordinate body orientation against the current, capture food, or escape from predators using relatively simple tectal circuitries (retina → TeO → motor outputs).
source: Yet zebrafish larvae can coordinate body orientation against the current, capture food, or escape from predators using relatively simple tectal circuitries (retina → TeO → motor outputs) (Del Bene et al., 2010; Grama and Engert, 2012; Barker and Baier, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Visuo-motor processing at the level of tectum in zebrafish may be comparable to the circuitry involved in saccadic eye movements in mammals.
source: Such visuo-motor processing at the level of tectum (without reaching the forebrain) may be comparable to the circuitry involved in saccadic eye movements in mammals (Yamamoto and Bloch, 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison made by the authors and supported by a citation.

claim: Larval and early juvenile zebrafish behaviors are largely dependent on the tectal circuitries.
source: It is possible that larval and early juvenile zebrafish behaviors are largely dependent on the tectal circuitries, and the visual system involving telencephalic circuitry becomes more important at later stages.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental observations.

claim: The visual system involving telencephalic circuitry becomes more important at later stages in zebrafish.
source: It is possible that larval and early juvenile zebrafish behaviors are largely dependent on the tectal circuitries, and the visual system involving telencephalic circuitry becomes more important at later stages.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the developmental observations.

claim: The presence of 'two visual systems' terminating in the mammalian cortex has been proposed based on mammalian studies.
source: Based on mammalian studies, the presence of 'two visual systems' terminating in the mammalian cortex has been proposed (Schneider, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: One visual system is called the 'thalamofugal' or 'geniculate' pathway, in which retinal inputs reach the striate visual cortex (V1) via the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: One system is called the 'thalamofugal' or 'geniculate' pathway, in which retinal inputs reach the striate visual cortex (V1) via a thalamic nucleus (lateral geniculate nucleus in the case of mammals).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian visual pathways.

claim: The other visual system is called the 'tectofugal' or 'extrageniculate' pathway, in which retinal inputs reach the extrastriate visual cortex via the tectum and another thalamic nucleus.
source: The other is called the 'tectofugal' or 'extrageniculate' pathway, in which retinal inputs reach the extrastriate visual cortex via two intermediate structures, the tectum (superior colliculus in mammals) and another thalamic nucleus (pulvinar in primates and lateral posterior nucleus in other mammals like rodents).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian visual pathways.

claim: Most studies in non-mammals have been interpreted based on the notion of 'two visual systems'.
source: Since then, most studies in non-mammals have been interpreted based on this notion of 'two visual systems' (Hall and Ebner, 1970; Karten and Hodos, 1970; Riss and Jakway, 1970; Ingle, 1973; Karten et al., 1973; Hagio et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Researchers have never reached a consensus on the evolutionary history of the tectofugal pathways.
source: However, researchers have never reached a consensus on the evolutionary history of the tectofugal pathways.
evidence: This reflects the current state of scientific debate.

claim: The debates on tectofugal pathways have often been related to unsolved homology of the target pallial areas.
source: The debates have often been related to unsolved homology of the target pallial areas.
evidence: This is stated as a reason for the ongoing debates.

claim: The current study does not solve the problem of pallial homology.
source: Our study does not solve the problem of pallial homology, but it strongly suggests that the tectofugal pathways in amniotes and teleosts are not homologous.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the scope of the current study.

claim: The tectofugal pathways in amniotes and teleosts are not homologous.
source: Our study does not solve the problem of pallial homology, but it strongly suggests that the tectofugal pathways in amniotes and teleosts are not homologous.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on the developmental data.

claim: In tetrapods, the neuronal cell bodies giving rise to the pallial projections are located in the thalamus.
source: In tetrapods, the neuronal cell bodies giving rise to the pallial projections are located in the thalamus, even though their projection targets differ between the major tetrapod groups.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about tetrapod neuroanatomy.

claim: The data clearly suggest that many (if not all) of the PG neurons are not part of the thalamus, but have a mesencephalic origin.
source: In contrast, our data clearly suggest that many (if not all) of the PG neurons are not part of the thalamus, but have a mesencephalic origin.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the cell lineage tracing experiments.

claim: In terms of regional homology, the teleost PG is not homologous to the amniote thalamus that is considered to be of forebrain origin.
source: Thus, in terms of regional homology, the teleost PG is not homologous to the amniote thalamus that is considered to be of forebrain origin.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the developmental origin data.

claim: There exists a possibility that some PG cells come from a forebrain territory.
source: There exists a possibility that some PG cells come from a forebrain territory, as suggested by previous studies (Wullimann and Rink, 2001; Wullimann and Rink, 2002; Ishikawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is acknowledged as a possibility based on previous research.

claim: Cladistics analysis reveals the lack of evolutionary continuity of the thalamo-pallial projections.
source: Nonetheless, in addition to the developmental criteria, the cladistics analysis also reveals the lack of evolutionary continuity of the thalamo-pallial projections as detailed below.
evidence: This is stated as an additional line of evidence supporting the main conclusion.

claim: Substantial tectofugal visual pathways to the pallium are observed only in amniotes and teleosts, and not in the intermediate taxa.
source: Substantial tectofugal visual pathways to the pallium are observed only in amniotes and teleosts, and not in the intermediate taxa (Figure 9).
evidence: This is stated as a comparative observation and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: Basal groups of the actinopterygians have a poorly developed pallial connectivity, and afferent projections from the thalamic region seem to terminate in the ventral portion of the telencephalon.
source: Similarly, basal groups of the actinopterygians also have a poorly developed pallial connectivity, and afferent projections from the thalamic region seem to terminate in the ventral portion of the telencephalon (Albert et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 1999; Holmes and Northcutt, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In Polypterus, visual projection to the pallium is mediated via the nucleus medianus of the posterior tuberculum (MTP).
source: Furthermore, in Polypterus, visual projection to the pallium is mediated via the nucleus medianus of the posterior tuberculum (MTP; Figure 9), which is considered to be uniquely derived in this group and not homologous to any known pathways in tetrapods (Northcutt et al., 2004; Northcutt, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 9.

claim: The MTP in Polypterus is considered to be uniquely derived in this group and not homologous to any known pathways in tetrapods.
source: Furthermore, in Polypterus, visual projection to the pallium is mediated via the nucleus medianus of the posterior tuberculum (MTP; Figure 9), which is considered to be uniquely derived in this group and not homologous to any known pathways in tetrapods (Northcutt et al., 2004; Northcutt, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There are more than two ascending pathways, with a variable abundance of each pathway depending on species.
source: Indeed, there are more than two ascending pathways, with a variable abundance of each pathway depending on species (Riss and Jakway, 1970; Graybiel, 1972; Benevento and Standage, 1983; Gamlin and Cohen, 1986; Albert et al., 1999; Wild and Gaede, 2016; Heap et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: These observations strongly suggest that the teleost and amniote pathways are not homologous to one another, but have evolved independently.
source: In combination, these observations strongly suggest that the teleost and amniote pathways are not homologous to one another, but have evolved independently.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the comparative analysis.

claim: The amniote thalamo-pallial projections (thalamocortical projections in mammals) are intra-forebrain projections, from the dorsal diencephalon to the dorsal telencephalon.
source: The amniote thalamo-pallial projections (thalamocortical projections in mammals) are intra-forebrain projections, from the dorsal diencephalon to the dorsal telencephalon.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about amniote neuroanatomy.

claim: The PG-pallial projection in teleosts is a midbrain-forebrain projection.
source: In contrast, our data suggest that the PG-pallial projection in teleosts is a midbrain-forebrain projection, and that a non-forebrain cell population can play an equivalent role to the thalamocortical projection neurons (conveying sensory information to the pallium).
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the developmental origin data.

claim: A non-forebrain cell population can play an equivalent role to the thalamocortical projection neurons in conveying sensory information to the pallium.
source: In contrast, our data suggest that the PG-pallial projection in teleosts is a midbrain-forebrain projection, and that a non-forebrain cell population can play an equivalent role to the thalamocortical projection neurons (conveying sensory information to the pallium).
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the functional and developmental data.

claim: The external part of the IL, another teleost-specific multi-sensory integration center, is also derived from the mesencephalon.
source: We have previously shown that the external part of the IL, another teleost-specific multi-sensory integration center (Rink and Wullimann, 1998; Shimizu et al., 1999; Ahrens and Wullimann, 2002; Yang et al., 2007), is also derived from the mesencephalon (Bloch et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous research and supported by citations.

claim: The teleost lineage has taken an evolutionary path different from amniotes, recruiting more mesencephalic structures for sensory processing.
source: More studies are needed to determine the functions of PG and IL, but these data indicate that the teleost lineage have taken an evolutionary path different from amniotes, recruiting more mesencephalic structures for sensory processing.
evidence: This is a major conclusion based on the comparative developmental data.

claim: Unexpected diversity of dopamine systems has been demonstrated, despite their involvement in similar physiological/behavioral properties across vertebrate groups.
source: In addition to the variation in neuronal connectivity that we reveal here, we have already demonstrated unexpected diversity of dopamine systems, despite their involvement in similar physiological/behavioral properties across vertebrate groups (Fontaine et al., 2015; Yamamoto et al., 2015; Yamamoto et al., 2017; Yamamoto and Bloch, 2017).
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous research and supported by citations.

claim: Striedter and Northcutt (2020) have pointed out a number of examples of convergent evolution across vertebrate taxa.
source: Recently, Striedter and Northcutt, 2020 have also pointed out a number of examples of convergent evolution across vertebrate taxa, in agreement with our hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to recent research.

claim: Vertebrate brains have tremendously diversified across taxa during evolution.
source: Taking all these data into consideration, vertebrate brains have tremendously diversified across taxa during evolution, and many more similarities are due to convergent evolution than previously thought.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion based on the current study and previous research.

claim: Many more similarities in vertebrate brains are due to convergent evolution than previously thought.
source: Taking all these data into consideration, vertebrate brains have tremendously diversified across taxa during evolution, and many more similarities are due to convergent evolution than previously thought.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion based on the current study and previous research.

claim: The majority of PG cells are derived from the midbrain in zebrafish.
source: However, our cell lineage study in zebrafish reveals that the majority of PG cells are derived from the midbrain, unlike the amniote thalamus.
evidence: This is a major finding of the study based on cell lineage tracing experiments.

claim: The PG projection neurons develop gradually until late juvenile stages.
source: We also demonstrate that the PG projection neurons develop gradually until late juvenile stages.
evidence: This is a major finding of the study based on developmental observations.

claim: Teleost PG, as a whole, is not homologous to the amniote thalamus.
source: Our data suggest that teleost PG, as a whole, is not homologous to the amniote thalamus.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on developmental origin data.

claim: The thalamocortical-like projections evolved from a non-forebrain cell population.
source: Thus, the thalamocortical-like projections evolved from a non-forebrain cell population, which indicates a surprising degree of variation in the vertebrate sensory systems.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study based on the developmental and comparative data.

claim: There is a surprising degree of variation in the vertebrate sensory systems.
source: Thus, the thalamocortical-like projections evolved from a non-forebrain cell population, which indicates a surprising degree of variation in the vertebrate sensory systems.
